plan.title: QuantSeq 3' liver DE: treated vs control
plan.analytical_narrative:
The input is a single 12,000-gene x 6-sample raw integer count matrix (counts.csv, gene symbols in column 1, one column per sample) with a 6-row metadata.csv carrying a single `condition` factor: 3 treated vs 3 control human liver samples, unpaired, one batch. The question is purely 'which genes differ between treated and control', so the plan is short and count-based.

Two library facts drive the method choice. First, this is a Lexogen QuantSeq FWD 3' tag-seq library: exactly one read per transcript molecule at the 3' end, with no transcript-length dependence. That makes counts directly comparable across genes within a sample without length normalization — TPM/FPKM must NOT be computed, and any length-aware machinery (goseq length bias correction, gene-length offsets, effective-length transcript quantification) is inapplicable and would inject a bias that is not present. It also means the counts are still integer counts of molecules, so a negative-binomial GLM on raw counts with a size-factor offset (DESeq2) is exactly the right model; the recommended QuantSeq analysis path is standard DESeq2/edgeR on gene-level counts. Second, 3' tag-seq libraries have a narrower dynamic range and a large tail of genes with near-zero counts, so independent filtering and shrunken effect sizes matter more than usual.

T1S1 runs the core DE: import the two CSVs, verify the sample columns align with the metadata rows, set control as the reference level, filter to genes with adequate counts, fit DESeq2 with ~condition, and emit a full results table with LFC shrinkage plus QC (library sizes, dispersion fit, PCA on VST, sample-sample distances). QC is embedded in the DE step rather than made a separate step because with n=3 per group the only QC decisions available are 'the groups separate or they do not' and 'a sample is an outlier or it is not' — both of which must be reported alongside the DE result to be interpretable. T1S2 is a robustness check with an independent method (edgeR quasi-likelihood, which is well suited to n=3 and controls type-I error better than exact tests), reporting concordance with DESeq2; a gene called by only one of the two frameworks is a weaker claim and the report must say so.

T2S1 takes the DESeq2 ranking (the full shrunken LFC-ordered list, not a thresholded subset) into rank-based GSEA against staged human hallmark and GO-BP gene sets, which are present in this environment for Homo sapiens. This is deliberately GSEA rather than over-representation, because with 3 vs 3 the FDR-significant gene list may be small or empty, and a rank-based test still yields a usable answer in that case. Enrichment is annotation, not the answer to the research question: if the gene sets are missing at run time the step reports that and the DE result stands.

Power is the dominant caveat throughout. Three versus three unpaired replicates gives reliable detection only for large, consistent fold changes; dispersion estimates lean heavily on information sharing across genes; and a single batch means treatment and any handling effect are indistinguishable. Every step is instructed to report effect sizes and adjusted p-values rather than gene counts alone, and to state the power limitation explicitly rather than presenting the hit list as complete.
